1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
8	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
9	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
10	We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
11	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
12	
13	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
14	\label{sec:generation}
15	
16	We construct generation chains using six generators spanning three model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, and \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}.
17	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8.2B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
18	
19	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
20	The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
21	In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
22	We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
23	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
24	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
25	The resulting dataset contains approximately 27{,}000 texts across all generators and depths.
26	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
27	
28	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
29	\label{sec:features}
30	
31	The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
32	Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
33	Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes).
34	This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the hypothesis that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
35	
36	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
37	
38	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
39	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than and architecturally independent of all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
40	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics:
41	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
42	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
43	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
44	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
45	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL, capturing the most predictable token---as generation depth increases, the floor of token-level surprise drops, reflecting the model's increasing confidence on its own outputs.
46	    Although entropy\_min shows near-zero marginal impact in leave-one-feature-out analysis ($\Delta$F1\,=\,+0.01\,pp), we retain it for completeness of the NLL summary statistics (mean, std, max, min) and because removing it does not improve performance;
47	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: proportion of tokens whose NLL exceeds the 90th percentile of the reference distribution (computed over $\mathcal{C}_0$), measuring how heavy-tailed the NLL distribution is relative to human text.
48	    The 90th percentile threshold follows standard practice in heavy-tail analysis \cite{ood_baseline}; sensitivity analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:tail-threshold}) confirms stable classification across thresholds from the 85th to 95th percentile.
49	\end{itemize}
50	
51	\paragraph{Surface features.}
52	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
53	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
54	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
55	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena}).
56	\end{itemize}
57	
58	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
59	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy\_std, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary.
60	This differential behavior---consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form---motivates combining both feature types.
61	As shown in \S\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.
62	
63	\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
64	\label{sec:evaluation}
65	
66	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
67	To evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the six generators is held out for testing and the remaining five provide training data.
68	We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.
69	
70	\paragraph{Classifier.}
71	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.
72	Gradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.
73	We use $n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, and learning rate $0.1$ for the 7-feature ensemble.
74	Baseline detectors (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}) use the same XGBoost framework with $n\_\text{estimators}{=}100$ and $\max\_\text{depth}{=}3$ to avoid overfitting their single-feature input.
75	LOGO F1 is stable across random seeds (mean\,=\,0.789, std\,=\,0.0009 over 5 seeds), confirming that results are not sensitive to classifier initialization.
76	Alternative classifiers (random forest, logistic regression) yield comparable performance (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}), confirming that discriminative power resides in the features, not the classifier.
77	
78	\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
79	The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, which weights minority classes (gen-1, gen-2+) equally against the typically easier gen-0 class.
80	We report per-class F1 scores and 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals ($n{=}1{,}000$ resamples).
81	For pairwise model comparisons (e.g., full features vs.\ ablated subsets), we use the \textbf{McNemar test} on disagreement tables.
82	For comparisons against detection baselines, we use \textbf{paired bootstrap} significance tests.
83	All reported $p$-values are two-sided.
84	We report six pairwise comparisons in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}; applying Bonferroni correction ($\alpha_{\text{adj}} = 0.05/6 = 0.0083$), all remain significant at $p < 0.001$.
85	Feature--depth correlations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) are computed on class-balanced subsamples (equal samples per depth class) to control for depth-class imbalance in the generation pipeline.
86	
87	\paragraph{Baselines.}
88	We compare the 7-feature ensemble against four single-score detection methods repurposed as ordinal depth predictors: Avg-LogProb, FastDetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars}, and LD-Score \cite{ld_score}.
89	Each baseline score is used as a univariate feature in the same XGBoost framework under LOGO cross-validation, ensuring a controlled comparison.
90	
91	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
92	Since TTR and hapax\_ratio are mechanically length-dependent, we verify that depth signal is not an artifact of systematic length variation.
93	We conduct three complementary analyses: (1) Spearman correlation between text length and each feature (requiring $|\rho| < 0.15$ for non-confounded features), (2) classification with length-normalized features, and (3) comparison on length-matched subsets.
94

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
We refer to the overall framework---features, classifier, and evaluation protocol---as \emph{depth fingerprinting}, distinguishing the method from the task it addresses.
No existing method addresses this task directly in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.41--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
We focus on non-paraphrastic continuation chains from base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned and RLHF models, which dominate web text, remain untested (Limitations).

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8.2B parameters).
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79, with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified).
In our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We characterize differential depth response across six generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8.2B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.79, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
    \item \textbf{Complementary analysis.} As a complementary analysis, we show that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather than curative tool.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, baseline comparisons, and the downstream utility experiment.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications, and a separate Limitations section addresses scope boundaries.

1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
5	
6	\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
7	\label{sec:results-classification}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.
10	
11	The 7-feature ensemble achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.789, significantly outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p<0.001$; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
12	Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
13	Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.
14	
15	\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
16	The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
17	However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
18	Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
19	Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+1.1\,pp to 0.811), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
20	A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
21	We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
24	Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).
25	
26	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
27	Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
28	Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

68	drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
69	while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).

72	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.

75	Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.
76	
77	\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
78	To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.789, significantly outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p<0.001$; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.
Text generated by larger models is more fluent, compressing feature margins and making depth distinctions harder.
Notably, adding Qwen3-8B data \emph{improves} classification on the original five generators (+1.1\,pp to 0.811), indicating that cross-scale diversity benefits rather than dilutes the training signal.
A volume-matched control confirms this gain is driven by generator diversity, not data quantity: upsampling the 4-generator training set to match the 5-generator count yields only +0.05\,pp, while the remaining +0.78\,pp (94\% of the total improvement) is attributable to the additional generator's distributional diversity.
We note that this gap may narrow with scale-matched training data; our current dataset contains $\sim$1{,}000 samples per generator regardless of scale.

\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution---the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts), while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Central-tendency and diversity features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show strong monotonic drift, while shape features (entropy std, tail decay) remain near-stationary.}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Individual-level Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show strong monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.558$, TTR $\rho = -0.542$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.475$),
while shape features show weak or negligible correlations (entropy std $|\rho| = 0.076$, tail decay $|\rho| = 0.089$).

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} reports ablation results.
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.789) significantly outperforms both surface-only features (TTR, hapax\_ratio; F1\,=\,0.729) and reference-only features (entropy mean/std/max/min, tail\_decay; F1\,=\,0.745; McNemar $p \approx 0$).
Permutation importance ranks hapax ratio highest (0.269), followed by entropy mean (0.164) and TTR (0.159).
Surface features capture vocabulary impoverishment; reference features capture distributional shift---neither subsumes the other.

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
To confirm that differential depth response is not an artifact of the Pythia-410M reference model, we compute features using three cross-family references: Pythia-410M, OLMo-2-1B, and Qwen3-0.6B.
All three achieve LOGO F1 between 0.80 and 0.82, with consistent drift directions across features.
The pattern generalizes across reference model architectures.

Leave-one-feature-out analysis confirms that 6 of 7 features contribute positively, with entropy\_max showing the largest marginal impact despite modest split frequency (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}
The ensemble outperforms every \emph{single} detection baseline in mean F1: +3.5\,pp over Avg-LogProb ($p < 0.001$, $\Delta$ CI [3.0, 4.0]), +7.9\,pp over LD-Score, +17.3\,pp over FastDetectGPT, and +22.1\,pp over Binoculars (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

The critical distinction is \emph{reliability}.
The ensemble achieves per-generator F1 ranging from 0.683 to 0.856 (std\,=\,0.058).
While this range reflects genuine difficulty variation across generators---particularly at larger scales (\S\ref{sec:results-classification})---the ensemble provides reliable performance even for the most challenging generator (Qwen3-8B: 0.683).
Each single detector captures partial depth signal---Avg-LogProb tracks mean perplexity shift, LD-Score captures character-level distributional change---but each fails on specific generator families.
The 7-feature ensemble aggregates complementary signals, producing stable performance regardless of the held-out generator.
The overall 95\% bootstrap CI [0.783, 0.792] reflects sampling precision of the pooled estimate, not cross-generator consistency.

\paragraph{Multi-detector ensembles.}
To test whether combining multiple detection scores yields stronger depth signal, we train XGBoost on all four baseline scores jointly (4-detector ensemble).

Adding our surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) to the 4-detector ensemble further improves performance to 0.805 [0.800, 0.809], the strongest configuration tested.
This confirms that our surface diversity features capture signal complementary to detection scores.
However, the 4-detector ensemble requires running four separate detection pipelines, while the 7-feature approach uses a single lightweight reference model (Pythia-410M) plus two vocabulary statistics.
The practical advantage of depth features lies in their interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern (\S\ref{sec:results-differential})---and computational efficiency, not raw classification accuracy.


\subsection{Downstream Utility: A Negative Finding}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All six generators are base (pretrained) models.
Web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models, whose generation distributions differ from base model continuations.

Chains are constructed with a single generator model per step.
Real-world web contamination likely involves heterogeneous generators at each depth, which could attenuate or alter the depth signal we observe.
We also do not evaluate robustness to human editing or post-processing of generated text, which is common in practice and may disrupt distributional features.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) suggest the phenomenon is not reference-specific.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
5	Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
7	Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
8	If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
9	We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.
10	
11	\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
12	Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
13	Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
14	This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
15	Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.
16	
17	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
18	The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
19	Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
20	Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
21	Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
22	Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.
23	
24	\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
25	Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
26	This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
27	The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.
28	
29	\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
30	Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
31	Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
32	We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
33	This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
34	The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.
35	
36	\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
37	Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
38	However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
39	Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
40	Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
41	The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.
42	
43	\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
44	While multi-detector ensembles achieve higher raw accuracy (0.805 with surface features added), depth features offer a single-model, interpretable alternative that reveals the underlying distributional dynamics of recursive generation.
45	
46	\paragraph{Same-family reference bias.}
47	Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M).
48	Cross-family references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), confirming that this generator's high detectability reflects its intrinsic generation patterns rather than reference-model family bias.
49

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer granularity.
Across six generators from three model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble combining both feature types achieves leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 of 0.79, with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
We also reported that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling, establishing that, in our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting functions as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization rather than a curative tool for data selection.

Future work should extend evaluation to instruction-tuned and RLHF models, frontier-scale generators (70B+), mixed-generator chains that better approximate real-world contamination, and multilingual settings.
All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication to facilitate reproducibility.

\label{sec:results}

We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.

The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.789 (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), the gen-0 class F1 (0.94) may be inflated; we therefore report a leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, F1\,=\,0.723) as the primary metric in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}.
Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.683 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.856 (Pythia-1B).
Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.
Note that gen-0 accuracy (0.94) may be inflated by shared seed texts across generators (see \S\ref{sec:results-baselines} for a binary evaluation excluding gen-0).

\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists at scales beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators.
However, cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B held-out F1\,=\,0.683 (CI [0.668, 0.694]), compared to 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   I am acting as an **independent scientific reviewer** for the `gen-depth-fingerprint` project (ordinal depth estimation in recursive LLM generation chains). My role is to independently verify experiment conclusions, review paper writing quality, and post findings via `reviewer_post_to_director`. I respond only to system notifications about completed workers and ROADMAP updates. All output must be in Chinese. I am read-only — I cannot modify files or run experiments.

   The project is targeting **EMNLP 2026 ARR (DDL: 2026-05-25)** with 10 days remaining. Round 2 review came back Borderline 3/5 with 4 Critical + 6 Major + 9 Minor issues. The team is actively fixing these.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Ordinal depth estimation**: Classifying text as gen-0 (human) / gen-1 (first LLM generation) / gen-2+ (recursive)
   - **Differential depth response**: Central-tendency features drift with depth, shape features stay stationary
   - **LOGO (Leave-One-Generator-Out)**: Cross-validation holding out one generator
   - **7-feature ensemble**: entropy_mean, entropy_std, entropy_min, entropy_max, tail_decay, ttr, hapax_ratio
   - **Gen-0 data leakage**: Wikipedia seeds shared across all generators → train-test overlap in LOGO for gen-0 class
   - **Binary F1 (gen-1 vs gen-2+)**: New primary metric (0.723) replacing 3-class F1 (0.789) after gen-0 leakage discovery
   - **Bootstrap CI vs per-generator std**: CI width measures sampling precision, not cross-generator consistency (C1 fix)
   - **4-baseline ensemble**: AvgLogProb + LD-Score + FastDetectGPT + Binoculars combined via XGBoost
   - **CORAL / Frank-Hall**: Ordinal regression methods tested against XGBoost multiclass

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/data/wiki_seed_1000.jsonl`** (remote server)
     - Contains 1000 Wikipedia articles shared as gen-0 seeds across ALL generators
     - CRITICAL: This is the source of gen-0 data leakage in LOGO evaluation
   
   - **`/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/scripts/review_baseline_ensemble.py`** (remote)
     - Exp A script: 4-group comparison (4-baseline, 4-baseline+surface, 7-feature unified, 7-feature original)

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer granularity.
Across six generators from three model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble combining both feature types achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.72 for leak-free depth discrimination, with per-generator std of 0.051.
We also reported that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling, establishing that, in our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting functions as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization rather than a curative tool for data selection.

Future work should extend evaluation to instruction-tuned and RLHF models, frontier-scale generators (70B+), mixed-generator chains that better approximate real-world contamination, and multilingual settings.
All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication to facilitate reproducibility.

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
As LLM outputs accumulate on the web, training corpora increasingly contain recursively generated text of unknown provenance depth.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text as human-written (gen-0), first-generation synthetic (gen-1), or deeper (gen-2+)---beyond binary detection.
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this complementarity achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.72 for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ depth discrimination ($p < 0.001$ vs.\ all baselines) across 6 generators from 3 model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).
In our setting, depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling, positioning depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All six generators are base (pretrained) models.
Web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models, whose generation distributions differ from base model continuations.
Validating that differential depth response persists under instruction tuning is a critical direction for future work.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale, but cross-scale classifier transfer incurs a moderate gap (held-out F1\,=\,0.683 vs.\ 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

We evaluate three prompt types (continuation, elaboration, rewriting; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}) but all share the same Pythia-2.8B generator.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms the depth signal generalizes, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Chains are constructed with a single generator model per step.
Real-world web contamination likely involves heterogeneous generators at each depth, which could attenuate or alter the depth signal we observe.
We also do not evaluate robustness to human editing or post-processing of generated text, which is common in practice and may disrupt distributional features.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) suggest the phenomenon is not reference-specific.
All seed texts are English Wikipedia excerpts; generalization to other languages and domains remains untested.

The negative downstream result (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}) is evaluated on causal language modeling only.
Other downstream tasks (classification, summarization, instruction following) may respond differently to depth composition.

Our analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p=0.9$). The relationship between sampling strategy and depth signal magnitude remains an open question.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
In 3-class evaluation, multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 (0.805 with surface features added vs.\ 0.789).
However, this advantage is driven entirely by gen-0 classification, where detection scores excel at human-vs-machine discrimination.
In the leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), the 7-feature ensemble matches the best multi-detector configuration (0.723 vs.\ 0.724), demonstrating that depth features capture the gen-1/gen-2+ distinction as effectively as four detection pipelines combined.
Depth features additionally offer interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern---and computational efficiency, requiring only a single lightweight reference model.

\paragraph{Same-family reference bias.}
Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M).
Cross-family references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), confirming that this generator's high detectability reflects its intrinsic generation patterns rather than reference-model family bias.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
We refer to the overall framework---features, classifier, and evaluation protocol---as \emph{depth fingerprinting}, distinguishing the method from the task it addresses.
No existing method addresses this task directly in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---confidence intervals spanning 0.41--0.82 in macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
We focus on non-paraphrastic continuation chains from base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned and RLHF models, which dominate web text, remain untested (Limitations).

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8.2B parameters).
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 of 0.79, with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
The practical advantage is reliability across unknown generators.

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified).
In our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We characterize differential depth response across six generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8.2B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves LOGO F1\,=\,0.79, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
    \item \textbf{Complementary analysis.} As a complementary analysis, we show that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather than curative tool.

5	Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
7	Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
8	If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
9	We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.
10	
11	\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
12	Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
13	Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
14	This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
15	Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.
16	
17	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
18	The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
19	Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
20	Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
21	Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
22	Finer-grained depth distinctions may be achievable for non-paraphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within $\sim$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries.
23	
24	\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
25	Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
26	This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
27	The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.
28	
29	\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
30	Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
31	Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
32	We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
33	This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
34	The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.
35
